108|chokhmat-shlomo|11|_: Section 11 — One who erred in Minchah, etc. Marginal note: Behold, in this there are views that one need not return and pray at Motzei Shabbos — what does he gain by praying more, etc.; and see what I wrote — clear proof for this in my novellae on the Gemara Pesachim 95b from what is written there: their reason is because of impurity of the threshold — he should return and do it in impurity, even though then there were only a minority impure and the majority performing were pure; and here the majority performing Pesach were impure and impurity was permitted or deferred in public — from this it is proven we do not follow the present but what was then at the time of the primary obligation, not at the time of make-up prayers; and as they say, the two make-up prayers of the first are for Motzei Shabbos; understand well.**** END BLOCK ****
108|chokhmat-shlomo|8|_: Section 8 — One who did not pray, etc. Marginal note: Behold, from this it is proven that forgetting is coercion; see in Magen Avraham what he discussed on this. And to me it seems to prove that forgetting is coercion: behold, initially it was difficult to me in what the Gemara says in chapter 4 of Bava Metzia (51b) — there it says Shmuel said: I say even according to R' Meir, etc. — R' Meir did not say there he certainly uproots; but here who will say he uproots? And it was very difficult for me how to interpret an explicit mishnah at the end of chapter 6 of Peah, thus: one who says 'I will harvest on condition that what I forget I may take' — he has [the right of] forgetting; and Rambam, Rosh, and Ra'avad explained from the power that any condition on what is written in the Torah — his condition is void. And it is difficult: behold there it is doubtful uprooting, for perhaps in any case he will not forget, and it is literally like 'on condition you have no claim of fraud against me.' And behold this would settle: one could say since we see R' Yehuda holds in monetary matters his condition stands — if so we see monetary law is lighter than prohibition; if so R' Meir holds even in monetary matters his condition is void — namely only where he certainly uproots; but in doubtful uprooting R' Meir concedes in monetary matters his condition stands. But in a matter that is not monetary, even in doubtful uprooting it is a condition on what is written in the Torah. But still, what shall we do with the topic in Gittin (64b) regarding 'on condition you eat meat' — there too it challenges that it was a condition on what is written in the Torah, and Ravina answers there too: it must be like other clothing and conjugal rights where he certainly uproots; but here 'you shall not eat' and 'you shall not divorce' — and so it was copied in Shulchan Aruch Avodah Zarah (simanim 38 and 144) — if so it is explicit that even regarding prohibition we say where it is not certain uprooting it is a condition on what is written in the Torah. And it is difficult: behold an explicit mishnah in Peah that this too is a condition on what is written in the Torah even though it is not certain uprooting. And at first glance this requires investigation; it must be explained that there it was in her power not to eat and not to divorce, and therefore anything in her power is not considered a condition on what is written in the Torah; but here it is not in his power not to forget, therefore it is a condition on what is written in the Torah. If so it works out if we say forgetting is literally coercion — then it is fine to say here, since it is not in his power, it was a condition on what is written in the Torah. But if we say forgetting is negligence — it must be proven that it was in his power to be careful not to forget; if so it was also in his power, and it is difficult why it would be a condition on what is written in the Torah when it is not certain uprooting. And certainly the matter depends: if it is literal coercion it was not in his power to guard against it; and if he was negligent it must be in his power to guard — for if it were not in his power to guard, that is not negligence. If so, if we say it was in his power not to forget, why was it considered there a condition on what is written in the Torah? It must be proven forgetting is not in his power, and it is proven it is literal coercion. And this is clear proof to me that forgetting is coercion; understand well.**** END BLOCK ****

And behold in siman 119, sk 5, he wrote: if one erred or skipped — meaning if one skipped the blessing entirely, or erred in not saying it as the Sages enacted, etc. And behold it would seem the matters contradict, but they do not contradict: for in siman 119 the intention is that one did not say something of the opening near the closing, or one closed or opened improperly; but if one opened and closed and mentioned something of the opening near the closing, even though one skipped in the middle, one need not return; and similarly Magen Avraham noted to see siman 59, where the intention is explained — that even if one said in the middle "He Who brings on evenings," one has fulfilled [the obligation]; and this is not like Ohr Zarua, who wrote; and it requires study there; examine well:
114|rabbi-akiva-eiger|5|_: Seif 5 — they return him. In my humble opinion, on Shabbat night if he forgot to say "Who causes the wind to blow" — they do not return him, for if he prayed only the seven-blessing [version] he has fulfilled, as stated in siman 268 in Magen Avraham, siman 15 — even in the seven blessings one does not mention rain. 114|rabbi-akiva-eiger|6|_: Seif 6 — that he began "You are holy." If he remembered after beginning the order of Kedushah, "Let Your name be sanctified" — he returns to the beginning, for the order of Kedushah is itself the third blessing, except that there are additional words in it. It is as if he began the third blessing — Gan HaMelekh, siman 152.
126|chokhmat-shlomo|4|_: (Seif 4): If the prayer leader erred when he prayed quietly he never returns, etc. I would say: see Magen Avraham what he wrote if he already completed his prayer, see there. And in my humble opinion the law is with the author of Biur Halacha, for it is evident from the wording of Shulchan Aruch that wrote "always returns" — and what is the wording "always"? One cannot say his intent is that even though he already stands in another place he returns to the beginning, for that would not need to write "always," for from the wording "returns" it already implies thus if he still stands in the place where he erred — what is the wording "returns"? Rather perforce the intent is that even though he already prayed further he returns to the beginning; and why write the wording "always"? Rather perforce the intent is always, even if he completed his prayer he returns to the beginning — and it is evident like the view of Biur Halacha; and so it is correct and requires good study.

131|chokhmat-shlomo|4|_: (Seif 4.) They are accustomed not to fall on their faces, not in the house of a mourner, etc. N.B. Here — regarding a deceased who was not given burial, in the matter that there is upon him no obligation of meals and no aninut — if they pray beside him, whether they say Tachanun or not, this depends on the two reasons why Tachanun is not said in a house of mourning: for the one reason, as it is written "And I will turn your festivals into mourning" — if so, in this case where the deceased lies and mourning has not yet taken effect upon him, one may say Tachanun; but for the other reason, that the measure of the Merciful One is extended — if so, all the more so after death before burial, that the measure of the Merciful One is extended with certainty — therefore one should not say Tachanun; so it appears to me in my humble opinion, correctly — examine well.
132|chokhmat-shlomo|2|_: Seif 2 in the gloss: and there are those who wrote to be careful to say pitum haketoret from the text and not by heart etc. Noda B'Yehuda: behold this is only on the understanding that is simple from what is written "whoever occupies himself with the portion of the olah, it is as if he offered an olah" — namely as if he offered it himself; so too he said regarding pitum haketoret "and if one omitted one of its spices he is liable to death." But according to what is written in my composition Orach Chayyim siman 1, and I proved that speech is not literally like offering but only as if he handed it to the kohen to offer — and so I found in Tosafos Shabbos — and it is recognized, for behold we are certainly impure from the dead and laymen; therefore he is certainly not liable to death if he hands incense missing one of its spices to the kohen; and perhaps this is Beit Yosef's reason, who brought Magen Avraham who wrote that one is not liable to death through speech; and perhaps it is from this reason, and understand well. (There) in the gloss: and they say orphan's kaddish after Aleinu etc. Noda B'Yehuda: behold a case came before me of one who had a doubt whether his father died on the 20th of the month or the 21st, and in any case on one of the two days he died; and he had a doubt whether his father died on the 19th or the 20th or the 21st; and on the 19th there were other yahrzeits and the one in doubt could not say kaddish; and on the 20th and 21st both doubts came to say kaddish, and this one in doubt claims that he is in doubt only on these two days that he will say the kaddishim on these two days, for then on one day he will certainly say as required, but on the second even on both days it remains doubt; therefore he is preferable. I was asked what his law is, and behold I saw in responsa Me'ir Netivim, who was asked on this and brought proof from Yevamos daf 96 regarding five whose offspring were mixed up, that we do not say one should perform yibum for all of them — it proves that if there is doubt that perhaps each one fulfills the mitzvah, it is preferable to what fulfills only one alone — see there. And in my humble opinion this is not proof: one, that they say there according to what Tosafos wrote in Pesachim regarding five whose Pesach hides were mixed up, who challenged there that behold semichah is not indispensable, and they answered that it is better one enter in doubt of karet than the majority act improperly — see there; it is implied explicitly from their words that there is a difference whether there were only two between whom there is doubt which acted improperly, and whether the majority acted properly — then they may not now act improperly for the minority who has doubt of karet; if so, here too perhaps there specifically because there are five in this manner, for it is impossible to fulfill the mitzvah with certainty except if one performs yibum for all; and if so, if we say to fulfill the mitzvah with certainty, only one would act and he is the minority among all; but if each performs yibum for one, they make each a doubtful mitzvah, and a doubtful mitzvah is also a mitzvah; therefore it is more preferable that the majority do a doubtful mitzvah than the minority do a certain mitzvah; and especially since there it applies per the one who says the mitzvah of yibum takes precedence — if so, if we say they all perform chalitzah, they would certainly act improperly; therefore since the majority would not fulfill the mitzvah of yibum but rather the majority would act improperly and perform chalitzah for their yevamah, therefore the majority may not act improperly for the individual who would act properly. And perhaps even there, if there were only two mixed up, we would say one should perform yibum for all and one would do a certain mitzvah rather than both do doubt; and even if we say that also with two the law is so that each performs yibum for one and chalitzah for one — nevertheless it is not similar to here, for if we say one performs chalitzah for all, then this one certainly acts improperly per the one who says the mitzvah of yibum takes precedence; if so, just as this one would do a certain mitzvah, so the two would certainly act improperly in reverse; and whatever they act improperly is only through this one acting properly; therefore what is the strength of this from that that this one should certainly act improperly that this one should certainly act properly — therefore both should do doubt. But in our case, if the one in doubt does not say kaddish on the 20th and 21st, he is not certainly acting improperly, for perhaps it is not his yahrzeit at all but his time was on the 19th of the month; if so, this one only does doubt of acting improperly, not certainly; and this second one would act certainly properly; and even though he did not say kaddish on the 19th, if so this one too would act certainly improperly — nevertheless what he did not say on the 19th did not cause him but another, and not through this one acting certainly properly did he cause this one to act certainly improperly, but through another; but through him there accrued to him only doubt of acting improperly; therefore here the certain is preferable to the doubt. But there, whatever this one acts improperly is only through this one acting properly; therefore what is the strength of this from that? And further, there it was active to say to this one to act and perform chalitzah in order to perform yibum for one — there the other can say "what is your certainty to me that I should act improperly so that you act properly, and my doubt is preferable to your certainty" — a person is close to himself. But here we do not force the second to act, but it is sit and do not act, and we are in doubt about the congregation praying there to whom they will give more kaddish, to this one or that one; therefore regarding others to whom both are equal one like the other, we say it is more fitting to give kaddish to this one who will say certainly than to this one who will say only in doubt; and in my humble opinion it is correct, not like the opinion of Sefer responsa Me'ir Netivim mentioned above, and understand well, and so I found.

154|chokhmat-shlomo|8|_: In the Rama gloss they practice enjoying many kinds of benefit from holy objects — not addressed; see Taz at note 7 what he wrote "were it not that I fear," etc.; see my chiddushim on Yoma 12b, as the gemara states there that "two" is not fit neither for the High Priest nor for an ordinary priest, because of "elevate in holiness and do not lower" — there I proved against his view; and especially what he said there (4) that he would have trouble in life, and it would be an inference that he would never be a priest — yet nevertheless "elevate in holiness and do not lower" applies to him; understand well. And what Taz wrote in the name of Maharshal that it is not called lowering as long as the sefer is inside it — and so wrote Magen Avraham in his name; and Bach brought that even this is lowering from holiness; understand well. And see my chiddushim on the Laws of Chanukah siman 671 what I wrote on this — proof for Bach that even this is lowering from holiness; understand well what I wrote on this and examine. And it appears to my humble opinion to bring proof to Maharshal's view that Taz brought above — that lowering from holiness for a time does not apply — from what we learn in chapter 4 of Sukkah 44b: since you say it is only taken by itself, obviously he is obligated in the willow in the lulav. And it is difficult: why does he ask — let him say it teaches us that even if he took it from the lulav he does not fulfill with it? And they answered: the reason is, in truth he does not fulfill this way if it is by itself; but one can say: since we hold it is forbidden to lower from grave holiness to light holiness, it is proven that this is contempt of a mitzvah; and therefore mitzvah objects may be discarded — that is, after their mitzvah time has passed; but during their mitzvah time they are forbidden for benefit and to use them from the power of contempt of a mitzvah, as written in Ne'ot Sukah and the like. And if so, even to use them for a light mitzvah is also included in contempt of a mitzvah. And if so, one can say: since the lulav is from the Torah in the borders one day, and the willow has no fundamental source from the Torah in the borders, and they make the lulav all seven as a remembrance of the Temple, and the willow one day — and if so it was a light mitzvah, and therefore one should not remove it from grave holiness to light holiness. And necessarily, with the lulav — even though this is not contempt, as is proven here, that while the books are still inside it is permitted to place in it also other books — either he cannot fulfill the willow, since it is only taken by itself; or if he took it from the lulav, again it is lowering from holiness for a time, and it is forbidden to remove it from grave to light, since it is still fit for the grave today. And one cannot say that in any event b'dieved why does he not fulfill — and behold the Tanna said he does not fulfill his obligation with the willow in the lulav, which implies even b'dieved; let one say it is a mitzvah that comes through transgression — and it is difficult for most poskim who hold Pasul even b'dieved. And what does he ask — perhaps while it is still fit for the mitzvah, as it is forbidden for mundane use, so too it is forbidden to change it to light holiness, which is also included in contempt of a mitzvah; and necessarily lowering for a time is not lowering; and since it is still possible to return it to the lulav, it is not considered lowering; and even in holiness it is permitted in such a case — how much more so with mitzvah objects. And it is proven like Maharshal's view, not like Bach; examine well.

168|chokhmat-shlomo|6|_: Seif 6—pat haba'ah b'kisnin one blesses borei minei mezonot etc. Footnote: I saw in Peri Megadim he was in doubt in law of pat haba'ah b'kisnin if one ate satiety measure whether liable to bless from Torah or only rabbinically. Ostensibly one can resolve this doubt from Talmud first chapter of Arakhin daf 4 where it says all are liable in zimmun—priests, Levites, Israelites—and challenges obvious, it is needed when they ate kodashim, lest one say Merciful One said and they shall eat those through whom atonement was made and behold atonement was made—teaches us and you shall eat and be satisfied Merciful One said and behold they are there—end Talmud; and it is hard: bread we do not find in sacrifice except in menachot—for in meat birkat hamazon does not apply and necessarily you find this novelty only in menachot—and in menachot there is oil and one does not fulfill with matzah and automatically no obligation of birkat hamazon at all—how does it say they are liable in zimmun; necessarily it refers to eating satiety measure through meal satiety and on this it says and you shall eat and be satisfied Merciful One said and behold they are there—if so it implies birkat hamazon applies from Torah. And do not say it refers to challot of thanksgiving that one fulfills with matzah and is not rich matzah and automatically liable in birkat hamazon—for in thanksgiving it is not relevant to say and they shall eat those through whom atonement was made for it is not for atonement. But per this our proof is not—for then you do not find it in minchah that it is for atonement except minchat choteh which is for atonement—and in minchat choteh there is no oil and it is not pat haba'ah b'kisnin; nevertheless one can prove reverse that all birkat hamazon on pat haba'ah b'kisnin is only rabbinic—for otherwise it is hard who compelled Talmud to explain reason that it was thought they are exempt from power of behold atonement was made—for then novelty would be only in minchat choteh alone; we also need to invent new reasoning that what is atonement does not have berachah—which is against reasoning [though true one can say from this proof for view of those who hold where one eats under compulsion he does not bless—and therefore it was thought since kohanim are compelled to eat it and Merciful One compelled them and he did not wish to eat only Torah forced him to eat—therefore it was thought berachah does not apply—therefore teaches since written and you shall eat and be satisfied and behold they are there; and per Talmud's conclusion one can say reverse even one who eats under compulsion blesses since written and you shall eat and be satisfied and they are there—and so on at length]. In any case it is hard why Talmud needed this extra—it should have answered it teaches in other menachot even though they did not eat in way of measure others establish on it—and if so it was thought they are exempt since it is pat haba'ah b'kisnin—therefore teaches since mitzvah in eating them mitzvah establishes him as kavua—therefore teaches kohanim are liable in zimmun even less than establishment measure since mitzvah in eating them mitzvah makes kavua as written in Talmud chapter 5 of Beitzah eating of Shabbat establishes for tithe and so many places; and proven from there eating of matzah is not considered casual only kavua and necessarily mitzvah established it—and if so teaches here too with kohanim mitzvah makes kavua and even less than measure others establish they are liable in zimmun—and therefore proven even real establishment is only rabbinic—and here itself is rabbinic enactment—cannot say regarding kohanim they enacted to bless also on less from power mitzvah considered it kavua for that is enactment on enactment which we do not do—and if so we do not say mitzvah makes kavua except in matter that is from Torah or at least establishment itself is from Torah—therefore it helps also to say mitzvah established it; but for birkat hamazon whose establishment measure itself is only rabbinic and from Torah does not depend on establishment only satiety—and what they enacted for pat haba'ah b'kisnin the measure as way others establish is only rabbinic—cannot say mitzvah established it for enactment on enactment; and there is proof from this it is only rabbinic; and I had place to extend but time did not allow—perhaps Heaven will grant another time to explain more—examine well.

190|chokhmat-shlomo|3|_: Seif 3: the measure of drinking wine to become obligated in a final berachah. See: behold in law there is a dispute among the poskim whether the measure of wine is a kezayit or a revi'it; it appears in my humble opinion there is clear proof that a kezayit suffices—from an explicit mishnah in tractate Me'ilah daf 15b: five things in an olah combine with each other, and six in a todah combine with each other—the flesh, bread, wine, etc.; and it is difficult: how does wine combine with flesh and bread—behold their measures are not equal, for this is a kezayit and that a revi'it; and it is explicit in the mishnah there later that whatever their measures are not equal they do not combine. And I saw in Tosafot Zevachim daf 109, brought in Tosefot Yom Tov on Me'ilah there, that they sensed this and answered: in bread that soaked in wine, which is a way of eating and is a kezayit—see there. But in my opinion their words are astounding—for behold the Talmud concludes in chapter 3 of Pesachim that in kodashim certainly heter combines with issur; and if so, why mention specifically in the mishnah five things in an olah and six in a todah—behold in all korbanot even wine of non-sacred or bread and flesh of non-sacred also combine for a kezayit for piggul, notar, and tamei, for in kodashim heter combines with issur. But behold the Talmud challenges similarly in chapter 3 of Pesachim regarding a nazir, as taught: from all that is made from the vine, wine for nazirite prohibitions combine with each other—and behold heter combines with issur; issur with issur is obvious; and it answers: heter combines with issur at once; issur with issur even one after the other; and if so, here too in what the mishnah teaches—five things in an olah, six in a todah—it deals with one after the other, and therefore heter combining with issur does not apply here; and if so, perforce it deals with one after the other; and if at once, in bread that soaked in wine the conclusion would be that even heter combines with issur; and perforce it deals with one after the other; and if so Tosafot's difficulty returns to its place—for behold their measures are not equal, and why do they combine? Perforce also wine's measure is a kezayit—and this is a great proof in my humble opinion; and understand well.
194|chokhmat-shlomo|2|_: Seif 2 — three who ate and one of them went out to the market, they call him, etc. It appears to me from this that if he does not join and answer with them he cannot invite zimun, even though at first they ate together and became obligated in zimun — he cannot invite zimun without them; and this is not similar to prayer, for we hold that if one began with Avot among ten he finishes, and many similar cases there that if one began with ten he finishes; and here what he began to eat with three does not help — there must be three at the berachah of zimun itself. It is difficult for me from the sugya in Sanhedrin chapter 1 daf 8, where the tanna taught: zimun with three — what is zimun? If we say the berachah of zimun — but it was taught: zimun and berachat zimun with three; and if you say he is explaining — what is zimun? The berachah of zimun — but it was taught: zimun with three and berachat zimun with three, etc.; and it is difficult why he challenges, and why should we push more that the intention is regarding zimun for judgment where what he paired with berachat zimun is not relevant; rather he should have explained as we thought regarding zimun in birkat hamazon, and what he doubled is when if he had written only one of them one would have thought he teaches only regarding the essence of the law that zimun requires three — to exclude if at first there were not three, to exclude from what we thought that zimun does not require three at all; therefore he teaches that from the outset of the law zimun requires three. Nevertheless it is possible that even if at first they ate with three it suffices, even though at the time of blessing there are not three they can invite zimun; therefore he teaches in the doubling that zimun requires three and it is not enough that there were three at first, only berachat zimun with three — at the time of blessing itself we require three; and why he challenges requires further study. From this it is further difficult for me on what Magen Avraham wrote in siman 191 explaining Tur's words, that behold the Sages were strict in zimun on a fourth berachah — meaning on the body of birkat hamazon that one discharges his fellow, which applies only in zimun with the Name; if so it is difficult why the Gemara challenges — let us say zimun refers to the body of birkat hamazon to discharge one's fellow, and berachat zimun refers to the berachah n'varech she'achalnu, etc.; and if he had written only one, one could say only n'varech requires three but the body of birkat hamazon to discharge one's fellow does not require three; therefore he teaches both to inform us that zimun means discharging one for his fellow in the body of birkat hamazon, and this came and revealed that; and the intention of zimun would be like there in Tur — what he wrote regarding zimun on a fourth berachah; and why he challenges requires further study — examine well.
